source: Talmy (1988) Force Dynamics in Language and Cognition, Cognitive Science 12(1); read as reprinted in Toward a Cognitive Semantics vol. 1 ch. 7
finding: Section 6 extends force dynamics to social forces. Talmy says one sentient entity's communication, read as a reason to act, is cast as pressure on another. Urge, persuade, give in, relent, refuse sit in the same force table as physical try, succeed, give way, withstand.
numbers: No experiments. Table 26 puts communicative rows (urge/be reluctant, persuade/relent, strike out/refuse) beside physical rows (try, manage, give way, fail, withstand). Examples: peer pressure; 'The gang pushed him to do things he didn't want to.'
quote: the same force-dynamic sequence ... underlies a new set of lexical items and constructions with interpersonal reference
limits: Linguistic analysis from examples only. Closes critique gap 5 on the primary text. Later critiques (Goddard, Deane) are still second-hand.
agent_relevance: A social or persuasion step can be tagged with the same slots (who pushes, who resists, who yields) as a physical one. A tagging scheme, not a tested method.

source: Talmy (1988) Force Dynamics in Language and Cognition, section 8 (argumentation and discourse expectation)
finding: Talmy treats argumentation as force dynamics. Each point can push toward or against a conclusion and overcome or be overcome. Closed-class 'force-dynamic logic gaters' (yes but, besides, nevertheless, moreover, granted, after all, even so) steer the argument state. He also describes 'vector reversal': two speakers agree on the outcome but assume opposite force directions (the 'For Chinese students only' email; the 'I was spared' Seder joke).
numbers: No data. Gaters named: yes but, besides, nevertheless, moreover, granted, instead, all the more so, whereas, on the contrary, after all, even so. Two worked discourse examples (47, 48).
quote: each such point can in turn oppose or reinforce another point and overcome or be overcome by it
limits: Descriptive. Talmy says 'future expositions are planned' for argumentation; we found none that operationalise it. Links to Argumentation and defeasible rules and Argument mapping in this run.
agent_relevance: Gives a force reading of rebuttal moves: a counter-point is an antagonist that blocks or is blocked. Could label objections as blockers or reinforcers. Untested.

source: Wolff, Barbey and Hausknecht (2010) For want of a nail: How absences cause events, J. Exp. Psychol. General 139(2):191-221
finding: Full text opened. Force theory says an absence is causal when a force is removed (double prevention, release) or when a virtual force is not realised. Four experiments, all one lab. Double-prevention chains were mostly described as ALLOW or CAUSE-by-absence, as predicted, but the B-to-C link split and 'None of the above' was often modal.
numbers: Exp 1 N=30 (Emory undergraduates), 5 animations; manipulation check: double-prevention description chosen 3% and 17% for CAUSE/CAUSE and CAUSE/PREVENT but 97%, 73%, 80% for P/P-1, P/P-2, P/P-3. Exp 2 N=75, 8 chains. Exp 3 N=36, 10 chains with virtual forces. Exp 4 N=48, 90 real sentences (9 types x 10). Theory predicts double prevention gives ALLOW 62% / CAUSE 38%; CAUSE-then-ALLOW chains ALLOW 76% / CAUSE 24%.
quote: people were willing to describe a causal chain with CAUSE and ALLOW
limits: Same lab as the theory; undergraduates; forced choice among four sentences; authors admit one result differed from prediction (timing in double preventions). No independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Strongest human data on absence causes and double prevention. Warns that ambiguous cells have no single right label, so an agent should not be marked wrong for either CAUSE or ALLOW there.

source: Xiang, Bigelow, Gerstenberg, Ullman and Gershman (2025) Language models assign responsibility based on actual rather than counterfactual contributions, CogSci 2025 (3-page paper)
finding: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o and GPT-4 judged blame, credit and bonus for two agents lifting a box. The LLMs followed a production or force account (how much force each agent actually produced). Humans followed actual plus counterfactual effort. This is the nearest LLM test of a force-based model of responsibility (the Wolff 2007 line).
numbers: 55 scenarios; scale 0-10. Force model best fit LLMs. Failure: r=.35 (4o-mini), .70 (4o), .71 (GPT-4); success: r=.80, .58, .82. Humans best fit by the Ensemble effort+counterfactual model: r=.92 failure, .90 success. Reward task: Force model r=.73/.76/.81 failure, .71/.72/.95 success; humans Effort model r=.98/.97. With forces matched, LLMs gave equal responsibility; humans gave more to the harder-trying agent.
quote: LLMs primarily use force to assign responsibility, humans primarily use actual and counterfactual effort
limits: Short paper, one task (BoxLifters), numbers given in the prompt, no scaffold condition, only OpenAI models. 'Force' here is physical force = strength x effort, not Talmy's tendency slot.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 8: an LLM given force numbers blames by output, not by effort or what could have been. A scaffold that adds a counterfactual-effort step is a testable fix. Not equal-token tested.

source: Quillien, O'Neill and Henne (2025) A counterfactual explanation for recency effects in double prevention scenarios: commentary on Thanawala and Erb (2024), Cognition (in press)
finding: People usually call the productive cause a cause and deny that the double preventer is one (Lombrozo 2010; Henne and O'Neill 2022). Thanawala and Erb (2024) found event order changes these judgments. The commentary shows a Counterfactual Effect Size model reproduces the order effects if recent events are re-simulated more. So double prevention may not need two concepts of cause.
numbers: Model fitted to Thanawala and Erb Exps 3 and 4; reproduces all qualitative order effects. Parameter estimates reported (e.g. s=.53, 95% CI [.18,.85]). Original sample sizes not extracted.
quote: temporal order of events affects the extent to which people simulate counterfactual alternatives
limits: Model fit to someone else's data; the original Thanawala and Erb paper was not opened. It conflicts with the force-theory view that double prevention is simply ALLOW.
agent_relevance: Judgments on double-prevention cases depend on order and on what is easy to imagine. Do not hard-code CAUSE vs ALLOW; ask what the counterfactual alternative is.

source: Ates, Gokhale, Baral and others (2020/2022) CRAFT: A benchmark for causal reasoning about forces and interactions, Findings of ACL 2022
finding: A video question-answering benchmark built on Force Dynamics: questions ask whether one object causes, enables or prevents another's event, plus counterfactual questions. Pre-LLM neural video-QA models were far below humans. An oracle model given the symbolic scene came close to humans.
numbers: 58K question-video pairs from 10K videos. Human study: 481 questions to 101 adults, 56 kept; overall 76.60% (causal 71.27, counterfactual 83.07, descriptive 87.45). Neural baselines about 40-55% on the question types in the table; oracle BERT-D 86.20 and 84.90 on two settings.
limits: 2020-era models (LSTM-CNN, MAC, TVQA, G-SWM), no modern LLM or VLM; synthetic scenes; the force-dynamics link is the cause/enable/prevent verb labels. Human sample small after exclusions (56 of 101).
agent_relevance: Shows cause/enable/prevent labelling has been used as a benchmark design. A rerun with current LLMs on symbolic scene text would directly test gap 4. We found none.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Causal Evaluation of Language Models (CaLM), arXiv 2405.00622
finding: Large causal benchmark on the Pearl ladder. The Actual Causality (AC) task, about attribution and responsibility, is hard for all models. The authors say they did NOT evaluate probability of disablement (PD) or enablement (PE), the formal cousins of prevent and enable.
numbers: AC: GPT-4 average 65.6%, text-davinci-003 57.2%, GPT-3.5-Turbo 56.5%; GPT-4 with manual CoT 68.2%, short of their 80 threshold. Manual CoT gave much bigger gains on other tasks (top pairs 90-97%).
quote: probability of disablement (PD), and probability of enablement (PE) ... leave for future exploration
limits: Older models (GPT-4 2023, Claude 2). AC items come from a BIG-bench causal-judgement set. Not a force-dynamics test.
agent_relevance: Confirms no large benchmark covers enable/disable. Gaps 4 and 1 stay open for LLMs. Manual CoT adds only a few points on AC.

source: Almeida, Nunes, Engelmann, Wiegmann and de Araujo (2024) Exploring the psychology of LLMs' moral and legal reasoning, Artificial Intelligence 333:104145
finding: Eight human studies replicated on GPT-4, Gemini Pro, Claude 2.1 and Llama 2 Chat 70b. Study 8 replicates Icard et al. 2017 (how norm violation and causal structure change causal ratings). Only GPT-4 matched human cell means; LLM answers were less variable than human ones.
numbers: Study 8: GPT-4 r(14)=.68 [.28,.88], p=.004 with human cell means over 16 cells; other LLMs not significant; GPT-4 vs Gemini Pro r=.60. Human SD about 1.8-2.1 vs LLM mean SD 1.2-1.7. 100 responses per model.
quote: models differ amongst themselves as to their overall alignment
limits: Only 16 cells. Older model versions. Causal structure here is conjunctive vs disjunctive, not force dynamics. Cheung 2026 chain responsibility (B over A) was not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partial: LLM causal ratings track humans weakly to moderately and are over-regular. Do not trust one LLM blame number; sample several.

source: Yu and Zhou (2026) Caliper: Probing lexical anchors versus causal structure in LLMs, arXiv 2606.04915
finding: Replacing variable names with placeholders (X1, X2) while keeping the causal graph lowers accuracy in almost all model-benchmark cells, so much causal accuracy is lexical. A 5-step structured scaffold (list graph edges, write the do-operator, parseable answer) narrowed the gap mainly by hurting the normal condition on small models.
numbers: Direct prompting, mean of 5 local models on CLadder interventional rung: P0 (named variables) 62.6%, P1 (placeholders) 55.6%, gap -7.0 pp. Scaffold: P0 57.2, P1 53.4, gap -3.8. CausalCoT: P0 30.9 with 48.1% unparseable answers. Few-shot gap -1.4 pp. Local-set gaps: -7.6 (CLadder), -27.0 (CRASS), -11.1 pp (e-CARE); nine frontier models -29.6 CRASS, -18.0 e-CARE; DeepSeek-R1 -3.2 / -15.7 / -15.1.
quote: Current instruction-tuned LLMs, evaluated zero-shot, show little evidence of structural causal reasoning once lexical anchors are removed.
limits: Models 3.8B-671B, zero-shot; not a force-slot scaffold; token budgets not matched.
agent_relevance: A structured causal scaffold can lower accuracy at small scale. Any force-slot test must report the normal-condition accuracy as well as the gain, and check parse failures.

source: Carro and Lagnado (2026) Human attribution of causality to AI across agency, misuse and misalignment, arXiv 2603.13236
finding: Human (Prolific) vignettes on chains of human, AI and developer. High or moderate AI agency gave the AI more causal responsibility; low AI agency gave it to the human despite distance. Splitting the AI into LLM and agentic tool, the agentic part was judged more causal. No LLM was the judge.
numbers: Studies with 50, 159, 128 (64 per condition), 160 and 160 Prolific participants.
limits: Human data only. Same Lagnado group as the Cheung 2026 result in K06. Does not test LLM blame ratings.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 still open for LLM judges. A ready human baseline for agent-chain blame.

source: Kankowski, Solstad, Zarriess and Bott (2025) Implicit causality-biases in humans and LLMs as a tool for benchmarking LLM discourse capabilities, arXiv 2501.12980
finding: German implicit-causality verbs (who is blamed in an explanation) tested on GPT-2, mGPT and BLOOM 0.35-6.4B against a human sentence-continuation study. Only the largest monolingual BLOOM showed a human-like coreference bias. No LLM showed the explanation bias humans show.
numbers: Human experiment: 52 participants, 2,080 continuations. LLMs: German GPT-2, mGPT, BLOOM 0.35B, 1.5B, 6.4B.
quote: no LLM displayed the explanation bias usually found for humans
limits: Small older models, German, no GPT-4-class model. Verb-level causal bias, not force dynamics.
agent_relevance: Verb-level causal semantics is not reliably absorbed by small LMs; silent on current frontier models.

source: Oba and Sugawara (2026) CxMP: A linguistic minimal-pair benchmark for constructional understanding in language models, arXiv 2602.21978
finding: Nine construction types including caused-motion and let-alone, as minimal pairs (43k items) written with GPT-5 and checked by humans. Syntax is learned early; constructional meaning only gradually and stays limited even in large models. It covers caused-motion but no let/make/prevent/help verbs.
numbers: Human validation: 168 Prolific participants, 896 items, majority-vote accuracy 96.65%, full agreement 83.59%; caused-motion 112 items, 100% majority. Models: GPT-2, RoBERTa, Pythia, Llama-3.1 8B/70B base and instruct, GPT-5.
limits: Per-model caused-motion accuracy not extracted. Closest benchmark design for gap 6, still not force-dynamic verbs.
agent_relevance: Shows how a force-dynamic verb minimal-pair set (let vs make vs prevent) could be built. None exists.

source: Gjerde, Cheung and Lagnado (2025) Reasoning about affordances: causal and compositional reasoning in LLMs, arXiv 2502.16606
finding: Tool-substitution task needing causally relevant object properties. GPT-4o with chain-of-thought matched humans; GPT-3.5 did not. A distractor condition hurt humans and models; an image condition hurt Claude 3.5 only.
numbers: 20 tasks, 4 options each. GPT-4o with CoT mean accuracy 85%, 0.8 points below humans; GPT-3.5 significantly lower (30% vs 80% on the saucepan item). F(2,267)=668.3 for model type.
limits: Affordances and property reasoning, not force dynamics. Preregistered, Prolific adults (N not extracted).
agent_relevance: Adjacent evidence that CoT lets a strong model reason about physical and causal properties at human level. Weak support for gap 7 by analogy only.

source: Search log, gap 2: replication of Butnaru et al. (2026) M-heuristic result
finding: No replication, follow-up or second LLM family test of 'Larry Caused the Car to Stop' was found. The only hit is the original paper. Whether the 188/188 prompt-the-rule result holds for Claude or GPT-4-class models, or with a short principle prompt, is unknown.
numbers: One WebSearch plus OpenAlex title searches; OpenAlex then hit its daily budget and the arXiv API returned 429, so absence is weak evidence.
limits: Search-only, not a source reading. The paper itself was opened by the cross-checker.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open. Cheap experiment: 188 items, three prompt lengths, equal tokens.

source: Search log, gap 3: independent replication of Wolff and Barbey (2015) composition table
finding: WebSearch, Europe PMC and OpenAlex found no independent-lab replication or failed replication of the cause/allow/prevent composition results, and no LLM test of composed relations. Closest: the theory's own lab (Wolff 2010, N=30, 75, 36, 48) and CRAFT (2020), which is not composition.
numbers: Europe PMC query for force theory/dynamics with causation 2016-2026 returned only Khemlani et al. 2020, Gardenfors 2020 and a 2026 Cognitive Science chain-responsibility paper (PMC13752550, not opened).
limits: Absence of evidence; OpenAlex budget exhausted mid-session.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open. Treat the composition table as one lab's result.

source: Search log, gap 7: force-dynamic or blocker-identification scaffolds for planning and tool-use agents
finding: No paper found that prompts a planning or tool-use agent with an agonist/antagonist or blocker-versus-enabler scheme. Hits were generic: LLM planning surveys, a structural-causal-model planner (AAAI), adversarial-planning skills, hierarchical scaffolding with rollback.
numbers: One WebSearch. Hits: arXiv 2505.19683 (planning survey), 2509.13127, 2509.04731, 2505.13921, an AAAI SCM-agent paper (none opened).
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. Any test would be new.

source: Search log, gap 6: LLMs and force-dynamic verbs (prevent, let, help, despite) outside arXiv and Europe PMC
finding: No peer-reviewed study tests LLMs on cause/let/prevent/help/despite as force-dynamic categories. An unreviewed web note claims GPT-4 grasps force-dynamic concepts but misreads agonist/antagonist in emotional sentences; its sources could not be traced. A 2022 master's thesis reportedly found no priming from force-dynamic primes to causal sentences. Adjacent: Kankowski 2025, CxMP 2026, CRAFT 2020.
numbers: Two WebSearches plus OpenAlex titles; the ACL Anthology search page was not queried.
limits: Web note and thesis are snippets, not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays mostly open; treat the web-note claim as unverified.

source: Henne and O'Neill (2022) and Lombrozo (2010), as summarised in Quillien et al. 2025: people deny the double preventer is a cause
finding: Second-hand through d05. In double prevention people usually say the productive cause (Pam threw the ball) caused the outcome and the double preventer (John fell into Tom) did not. This differs from Wolff's ALLOW/CAUSE split on animations and from the 50/50 in K04, and depends on whether the question asks about cause or allow.
numbers: No figures extracted from the originals.
quote: people tend to deny that the double preventer caused the window to shatter
limits: Primary papers not opened; read through the commentary.
agent_relevance: Supports treating double prevention as a flagged ambiguous case whose answer depends on question wording.
